# The microbial world

> *Most of the living things on Earth are too small to see, and almost all of them are harmless.
> This chapter sets the scale, sorts infectious agents into five kinds, and introduces the six
> questions the rest of the book asks of every one of them.*

## A matter of scale {#sec-world-scale}

A **microorganism**, or microbe, is any living thing too small to see without a microscope:
bacteria, archaea, fungi such as yeasts, and **protozoa** (single-celled eukaryotes that move and
feed like tiny animals). Viruses are usually included, although they are not cells. Medical
microbiology also covers **helminths** (parasitic worms), most of which are visible to the naked eye,
because they are infectious agents too.

The range of sizes is enormous. Try putting these in order before you read on.

<div data-island="rank-order" data-src="/diagrams/size-ladder.yml"></div>

Two consequences follow from size. The first is about seeing. A light microscope cannot separate
two points closer than about 0.2 µm, its limit of **resolution**, so bacteria are visible once
stained but viruses are not. Viruses were first seen in the late 1930s with the electron microscope, and
in clinical practice they are usually detected by their nucleic acid or their proteins instead.

The second is about growth. A small cell has a large surface area for its volume, so nutrients
reach every part of it quickly by diffusion. That is one reason bacteria can divide every 20 minutes
in good conditions, while your own cells take many hours.

## Five kinds of infectious agent {#sec-world-kinds}

All cellular life falls into three **domains**, defined by comparing the genes for ribosomal RNA
[@woese1990domains]:

- **Bacteria**, prokaryotic cells that include every bacterial pathogen in this book.
- **Archaea**, also prokaryotic, but with membranes and enzymes so different from bacteria that they
  form a separate branch. Archaea live in the human gut, but none is an established cause of
  human disease.
- **Eukarya**, cells with a nucleus. Fungi, protozoa and helminths belong here, alongside your own
  cells.

That close relationship matters. A bacterium has many structures your cells lack, so it is
relatively easy to attack without harming you. A fungus or a protozoan shares most of its machinery
with you, which leaves fewer safe targets. This is the sixth question of the book, *what does it
have that my cells lack?*, and the answer changes completely between the domains.

Two kinds of agent sit outside the tree of life. **Viruses** are not cells: a virus particle, or
**virion**, is a genome of DNA or RNA inside a protein coat, sometimes wrapped in a lipid envelope,
and it can only be copied inside a living cell. **Prions** have no genome at all. A prion is a
misfolded form of a normal host protein that converts other copies of the protein into the
misfolded shape, causing slowly progressive brain disease. Prions are rare, but they matter in
practice because they survive standard sterilisation, a point the *Detecting and controlling
microbes* chapter returns to.

Sort the descriptions below by their traits. None of them gives a name.

## Most microbes are harmless {#sec-world-harmless}

A **pathogen** is a microbe that can cause disease. Pathogens are a small minority of the microbial
world. About 1,400 species are known to infect humans [@taylor2001risk], out of millions of
microbial species, and most of those 1,400 cause disease only in some people, some of the time.

Far more microbes live with us without harm. The human body carries about 3.8 × 10^13^ bacteria,
mostly in the colon, compared with about 3.0 × 10^13^ human cells [@sender2016cells]. These resident
communities, the **microbiota**, digest food we cannot, compete with pathogens for space, and help
train the immune system. The *Microbes and their hosts* chapter describes them in detail.

::: {.callout-important}
## A common idea, corrected: "bacteria outnumber human cells ten to one"
This figure is still widely quoted. It came from a rough 1970s estimate that assumed every gram of
the gut contained as many bacteria as a gram of faeces. A careful recount in 2016 put the ratio at
about 1.3 bacteria for every human cell, with large swings: a single bowel movement can shift it
noticeably [@sender2016cells].
:::

Some microbes are useful to medicine in direct ways. The first recombinant human insulin, approved
in 1982, was made by *Escherichia coli* carrying the human insulin genes, and many antibiotics were
first found as products of soil bacteria. In Singapore, a bacterium is being used against dengue.
*Wolbachia* lives inside the cells of many insects. Male *Aedes aegypti* mosquitoes carrying it are
released in large numbers; when they mate with wild females, the eggs do not hatch, so the mosquito
population that transmits dengue falls. In a cluster-randomised trial in Singapore, releases reduced
the odds of laboratory-confirmed dengue by about 70% [@lim2026wolbachia].

## How microbes came to be blamed {#sec-world-history}

Until the late nineteenth century most doctors attributed epidemics to bad air, or **miasma**, and
to imbalances within the body. The idea that specific microbes cause specific diseases, the **germ
theory of disease**, was built from several lines of work:

| When | Who | What it showed |
|---|---|---|
| 1670s | Antonie van Leeuwenhoek | Microbes exist: he described "animalcules" seen through his hand-made lenses |
| 1840s | Ignaz Semmelweis | Hand washing with chlorinated lime cut deaths from fever after childbirth (the *Transmission* chapter) |
| 1860s | Louis Pasteur | Microbes cause fermentation and do not arise spontaneously in sterile broth |
| 1867 | Joseph Lister | Carbolic acid on wounds and instruments reduced post-operative infection |
| 1876–1882 | Robert Koch | *Bacillus anthracis* causes anthrax and *Mycobacterium tuberculosis* causes tuberculosis |

Koch's group also set out the logic for proving that a microbe causes a disease. In the form usually
taught, **Koch's postulates** require that:

1. The organism is found in every case of the disease.
2. It can be isolated and grown in pure culture.
3. The cultured organism causes the disease when introduced into a healthy, susceptible host.
4. The same organism can be recovered from that host.

The postulates are still a good way to think about causation, but many real pathogens fail them.
Some cannot be grown in culture at all, such as *Treponema pallidum*, the cause of syphilis. Many
cause disease in only some of the people they infect, so healthy **carriers** exist. Others need a
particular host factor, or cause disease only in combination with other microbes. Modern versions of
the postulates use genes rather than whole organisms: a gene is linked to virulence if inactivating
it reduces disease and restoring it brings disease back [@falkow1988molecular]. The case at the end
of this chapter follows one discovery that had to work around these problems.

## Same questions, different answers {#sec-world-questions}

This book asks the same six questions of every kind of microbe:

1. What is it built from?
2. How does it get energy, and what does it need to grow?
3. How does it copy itself and change?
4. Where does it live, and how does it spread?
5. How does damage happen, and how much is microbe versus host?
6. What does it have that my cells lack?

Each kind of agent gives a different answer to each question. The table below shows one example of
each kind. Every row returns later, in its own chapter.

| | Bacterium (*S. aureus*) | Virus (influenza) | Fungus (*Candida*) | Protozoan (*Plasmodium*) | Helminth (*Ascaris*) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Built from | Prokaryotic cell with a peptidoglycan wall | RNA genome, protein coat, lipid envelope | Eukaryotic cell with a chitin and glucan wall | Eukaryotic cell, no wall | Many-celled animal |
| Energy | Its own metabolism | None of its own; uses the host cell's | Its own metabolism | Its own metabolism, using host nutrients | Its own metabolism, feeding on gut contents |
| Copying | Binary fission; swaps genes | Copied inside host cells; segments reshuffle | Budding | Asexual cycles in humans, sexual stage in the mosquito | Sexual reproduction; eggs |
| Home and spread | Nose and skin; contact | Airway; respiratory particles | Skin, gut, vagina | Human liver and red cells; mosquito bite | Human intestine; eggs swallowed from soil |
| Damage | Invasion and toxins | Destroys airway cells; host inflammation | Overgrowth when defences fall | Destroys red cells; blocks small vessels | Heavy burdens obstruct the gut and impair nutrition |
| Unlike my cells | Peptidoglycan wall; 70S ribosomes | Viral enzymes for copying its genome | Ergosterol in its membrane; chitin and glucan wall | Some metabolic pathways | Nerve and muscle receptors unlike ours |

The rest of the book fills in this table. Part I covers the principles, starting with bacteria
because they show most of the ideas most clearly. Part II takes each group of organisms in turn.
